title: Division Undoes Multiplication
goal: I can solve a division fact by asking the multiplication question, like 56 ÷ 8 means 8 × ? = 56.

card.desc: Bailey learns that division is multiplication run backward: 56 ÷ 8 means 8 × ? = 56. In the Zoom class lesson she shares beans both ways (how many in each, how many groups), makes fact triangles for the 6–9 facts, and learns dividend, divisor, quotient and four more words; the after-class lesson has her do it on her own.

win: You turned every division into a multiplication you already know. That is real math thinking!

slides.title: On Your Own: Division Undoes Multiplication
slides.text: In class you learned that division asks a multiplication question. Now you do it on your own. It takes about 25 minutes, and it ends with Show What You Know.

slides.title: Teach it to someone
slides.text: Find someone at home. Teach them what you learned. Say it out loud before you go on.
prompts: What does 56 ÷ 8 mean? Use the words times what.
Tell them the two kinds of division question, with a dragon example for each.
In How to Train Your Dragon, who might need to ration food or allot supplies? Why?
starters: One kind asks how many in each, like …

slides.title: Remember the words
slides.text: Tap each card. Say the meaning before you flip it. Then flip to check yourself.

words.meaning: The number being divided: the total you start with.
The number you divide by: the number of groups, or how many go in each group.
The answer to a division problem.
Two operations that undo each other, like multiplication and division.
To give out something in small, set amounts so that it lasts longer.
words.example: When the winter was long, the Vikings had to ration their bread.

words.meaning: Supplies of food and other things people need, packed for later.
words.example: The ship carried provisions for a week at sea.

words.meaning: To give each person or group a certain share of something.
words.example: The chief will allot 6 arrows to each archer.

slides.title: The one big idea
slides.text: Turn every division into a multiplication question. Then use a fact you know.

slides.title: Ask the multiplication question
slides.text: Type the missing number.

items.no: Use the ×9 shortcut: 10 × 6 − 6 = 54.
Which 7s fact makes 49?

items.q: What number is hiding in this fact triangle? Type it.
items.no: Ask: 6 × what = 54?

items.q: To solve 64 ÷ 8, which question should you ask yourself?
no: That makes a much bigger number. Division of 64 gives an answer smaller than 64.
Taking away one 8 leaves 56. You need how many eights fit in 64.
8 + 56 = 64, so adding gives 56, not the answer.

slides.title: Eggs in the hatchery
slides.text: Fishlegs shares 48 dragon eggs equally among 8 nests. Make the groups: how many nests, and how many eggs in each one?
slides.why: 8 groups of 6 make 48. So 48 ÷ 8 = 6 eggs in each nest.
slides.hint: 8 nests means 8 groups. Then ask: 8 × what = 48?

slides.title: Each or groups?
slides.text: Read the story. Type each if it asks how many in each group. Type groups if it asks how many groups. Then solve it.

items.q: Hiccup has 56 fish. He feeds 8 fish to each dragon. How many dragons can he feed? Type each or groups.
items.why: You know how many go in each (8). The story asks how many groups: how many dragons.
items.no: Is 8 the number of dragons, or the fish for each dragon?

items.q: Now solve it: Hiccup has 56 fish and feeds 8 fish to each dragon. How many dragons?
items.no: Ask: 8 × what = 56?

items.q: Stoick splits 54 arrows equally among 6 archers. How many arrows does each archer get? Type each or groups.
items.why: You know the number of groups (6 archers). The story asks how many in each.
items.no: Is 6 the number of archers, or the arrows for each archer?

items.q: Now solve it: 54 arrows shared equally among 6 archers. How many arrows each?
items.no: Ask: 6 × what = 54? Try 5 × 9 = 45, plus one more 9.

slides.title: Sort by the quotient
slides.text: Tap a division card. Think of the multiplication fact. Then tap the box with its quotient.
slides.done: Every division card was a multiplication fact in disguise.

slides.title: Name it
slides.text: Type the word.

items.q: In 45 ÷ 9 = 5, the 5 is called the ____.
items.why: The quotient is the answer to a division problem.
items.no: It is the answer. The word starts with q.

items.q: In 45 ÷ 9 = 5, the 9 is called the ____.
items.why: The divisor is the number you divide by.
items.no: It is the number you divide BY.

items.q: The ship carried food and supplies for the long trip. Another word for those supplies is ____. (Use a word from your word cards.)
items.why: Provisions are supplies of food and needed things, packed for later.
items.no: It starts with p and ends with s.

items.q: Stoick will allot 8 fish to each family. Which word could replace allot?
items.why: To allot is to hand out shares.
no: Saving keeps the fish. Allot means to give out.
Counting does not give anyone fish.

items.q: Use the ×7 shortcut (×5 plus ×2). What is 7 × 8?
Use the area model. What is 36 × 7?
no: You added 7 instead of multiplying 6 × 7 = 42.
You forgot the ones box. Add 6 × 7 = 42.
Check the small box: 6 × 7 = 42, not 48. (6 × 8 = 48.)

sets.q: To solve 56 ÷ 7, ask: 7 × ____ = 56. Type the missing number.
What number is hiding in this fact triangle?
In 40 ÷ 8 = 5, which number is the divisor?
sets.why: The divisor is the number you divide by: 8.
no: 40 is the dividend, the number being divided.
5 is the quotient, the answer.

sets.q: Hiccup has 70 fish. He gives 7 fish to each dragon. How many dragons get fish?
Fishlegs shares 72 rocks equally into 9 bags. How many rocks go in each bag?
The answer to a division problem is called the ____.
sets.why: The quotient is the answer when you divide.

sets.q: The Vikings had to ration their bread all winter. What did they do?
choices: hid it in a secret pile
ate all of it on the first day
gave it out in small, set amounts so it would last
shared all of it out at one big feast
sets.why: To ration is to give out small, set amounts so supplies last.
no: Hiding a pile is not rationing. Rationing means sharing out small amounts.
That is the opposite of rationing.
Sharing it all at once means it is gone fast. Rationing makes it last.

sets.q: Which one shows inverse operations?
sets.why: Multiplication and division undo each other: 7 × 8 = 56, so 56 ÷ 8 = 7.
no: Both are multiplication. Inverse means one undoes the other.
Both are division. You need multiplication and division together.
Those are turn-around facts. Both are multiplication.

sets.q: To solve 63 ÷ 9, ask: 9 × ____ = 63. Type the missing number.
Which number is missing from this fact triangle?
In 54 ÷ 6 = 9, which number is the dividend?
sets.why: The dividend is the number being divided: 54.
no: 9 is the quotient, the answer.
6 is the divisor, the number you divide by.

sets.q: Stoick has 48 fish. He gives 8 fish to each dragon. How many dragons does he feed?
Hiccup shares 64 arrows equally among 8 Vikings. How many arrows does each Viking get?
The number you divide by is called the ____.
sets.why: The divisor is the number you divide by.
sets.no: It is the number you divide BY. It starts with d.

sets.q: Before the long voyage, the crew loaded provisions onto the ship. What did they load?
choices: food and supplies for the trip
sets.why: Provisions are supplies of food and needed things, packed for later.
no: Oars are part of the ship, not provisions.
Gold for trading is treasure, not provisions.
Provisions are what people need to live: food, water, supplies.

sets.q: Snotlout says 48 ÷ 6 = 9 because 6 × 9 = 48. What is wrong?
choices: You can't check division with multiplication.
sets.why: 6 × 8 = 48, so 48 ÷ 6 = 8. Snotlout used a wrong fact.
no: Check his fact: 6 × 9 = 54.
Subtracting takes away only one 6.
You can! They are inverse operations. His fact was just wrong.

sets.q: To solve 42 ÷ 6, ask: 6 × ____ = 42. Type the missing number.
sets.no: Use the ×6 shortcut: 5 × 7 = 35, plus one more 7.

sets.q: Find the hidden corner of this fact triangle.
In 35 ÷ 7 = 5, which number is the quotient?
no: 35 is the dividend, the number being divided.
7 is the divisor, the number you divide by.

sets.q: Fishlegs has 63 dragon eggs. He puts 7 eggs in each nest. How many nests does he fill?
Stoick shares 81 apples equally among 9 families. How many apples does each family get?
Multiplication and division undo each other. They are ____ operations.
sets.why: Operations that undo each other are inverse operations.

sets.q: The chief will allot 7 fish to each family. What will he do?
choices: give each family a share of 7 fish
sets.why: To allot is to give each person or group a certain share.
no: That is the opposite: allot means to give out.
Selling is trading, not giving shares.
Cooking does not give anyone a share.

sets.q: Which pair shows that multiplication and division are inverse operations?
sets.why: The division undoes the multiplication: 9 × 6 = 54, so 54 ÷ 9 = 6.
no: Both are multiplication: turn-around facts.
Both are division.
Both are multiplication, and they use different numbers.

practice.intro: Three tries on each one, but only your first try counts. Before you answer, ask yourself the multiplication question.

questions.q: What number is hiding in this fact triangle?
Which number is hiding in this fact triangle? Type it.
The tribe has 63 shields. They hang 9 on each wall. How many walls get shields?
Fishlegs reads 48 pages of his dragon book, the same number each night for 6 nights. How many pages each night?
In 54 ÷ 6 = 9, the number 54 is called the ____.
questions.why: The dividend is the number being divided: 54.
questions.no: dividend ÷ divisor = quotient. Which spot is 54 in?

questions.q: Which word means supplies of food and needed things, packed for later?
no: Ration is a verb: to give out in small amounts.
Quotient is the answer to division.
Divisor is the number you divide by.

questions.q: Snotlout says 49 ÷ 7 = 6. Which fact proves him wrong?
no: Adding does not check division.
That fact is wrong too: 7 × 8 = 56.
Subtracting one 7 does not check his answer.

questions.q: Stoick will allot the fish so every family gets some. Which word could replace allot?
questions.why: To allot is to hand out shares.
no: Saving up keeps the fish. Allot means to give out.
Counting does not give anyone fish.
Borrowing means taking for a while.

questions.q: To give out food in small, set amounts so it lasts is to ____ it. (Use a word from your word cards.)
questions.why: To ration is to give out small, set amounts so supplies last.

pages.title: Part 1: Word Power
pages.directions: Draw a line from each word to its meaning.

items.text: 1. Match each word to its meaning.
right: to give each person a share
the answer to a division problem
food and supplies packed for later
to give out small amounts so it lasts

pages.title: Part 2: Ask the multiplication question
pages.directions: Fill in the blanks. The multiplication fact gives you the division answer.

pages.title: Part 3: Fact triangle
pages.directions: Draw a fact triangle for 8, 7 and 56. Put the biggest number on top. Then write the two division facts.

items.text: 8. My triangle and my two division facts:

pages.title: Part 4: Story problems
pages.directions: Circle the kind of question the story asks. Then write the division fact and the multiplication fact that proves it.

items.text: 9. Stoick shares 48 fish equally among 8 dragons. How many fish does each dragon get?
10. Fishlegs has 54 dragon eggs. He puts 6 eggs in each nest. How many nests does he fill?
11. Hiccup reads 63 pages in 9 days. He reads the same number of pages each day. How many pages a day?
12. Explain why 56 ÷ 8 = 7. Use the words dividend, divisor and quotient.
13. Use ration or provisions in a sentence about life on Berk.

teacher.objective: Bailey understands division as the inverse of multiplication: she reads 56 ÷ 8 as "8 × ? = 56", tells a "how many in each" story from a "how many groups" story, and uses fact triangles for the 6–9 facts instead of adding the divisor over and over. She learns the words dividend, divisor and quotient.
materials: Zoom: share your screen with the Class lesson (teacher code 9110)
Whiteboard and marker (Jonathan), visible on camera
At Bailey's home (ask Tia to set out before the lesson): about 45 dried beans or counters and 6 cups or paper plates
6 index cards and a pencil for making fact triangles
Her book, How to Train Your Dragon
Packet (2 pages): printed later this week; it is assigned on Tuesday's task list

plan.do: Class slide 1. Confirm beans, 6 plates, index cards, pencil and her book are at her table. Quick fact: 8 × 7.
Class slide 2. Retell in order, name Hiccup's conflict type with an event as proof, share one new word and its clue.
Class slide 3. Four facts she will need (56, 54, 42, 63); she says the shortcut for each.
Class slide 4. She reads each card and makes her own sentence. Whiteboard: dividend ÷ divisor = quotient under 56 ÷ 8 = 7, left up all lesson.
Class slides 5–7. 24 beans onto 6 plates (how many in each), then piles of 6 (how many groups); quick check on which question a story asks.
Class slides 8–9. 56 ÷ 8 means 8 × ? = 56; she leads 72 ÷ 9 herself, saying each step first.
Class slide 10. She makes index-card triangles 8-7-56, 7-9-63, 6-9-54; cover a corner and say the fact, both directions.
Class slides 11–12. Question first, answer second; predict 42 ÷ 6 with a fact, then prove it with beans.
Class slides 13–14. Name dividend, divisor, quotient; spot Snotlout's wrong fact; lightning round of six division facts, saying the fact before each quotient.
Class slide 15. She names the clue word in each sentence and links allot and ration to division.
Class slide 16. Exit ticket out loud, then show the course page: tonight the After-class lesson (ends with Show What You Know, needs 90) and 10 minutes of reading.

watch: Adding the divisor over and over (8, 16, 24 …) to reach the dividend. Stop her kindly: "8 times what is 56? Which 8s fact do you know that is close?"
Mixing up divisor and quotient when naming parts. Point to the whiteboard line dividend ÷ divisor = quotient.
Writing the division backward (8 ÷ 56). Say: the top of the triangle, the biggest number, always comes first.
Using a fact that is one off (7 × 8 = 63). Have her check it with her ×7 shortcut: 5 × 8 + 2 × 8 = 40 + 16 = 56, so 7 × 8 = 56, not 63.
"I can't do it." Answer: "You already know the multiplication. Which fact is close?" Then wait.

packet_key.answer: dividend → the number being divided; divisor → the number you divide by; quotient → the answer to a division problem; ration → to give out small amounts so it lasts; provisions → food and supplies packed for later; allot → to give each person a share
Triangle with 56 on top and 8 and 7 at the bottom; 56 ÷ 8 = 7 and 56 ÷ 7 = 8
How many in each? 63 ÷ 9 = 7 pages a day; 9 × 7 = 63
Answers vary. Example: The dividend is 56 and the divisor is 8. 8 × 7 = 56, so the quotient is 7.
A complete sentence that uses ration (give out small, set amounts) or provisions (packed supplies) correctly.

teacher.notes: The class lesson ends at the wrap-up; Bailey takes Show What You Know on her own tonight at the end of the After-class lesson. Check her Formspree score before Tuesday. If it is under 90, open Tuesday's class by redoing the bean sharing with 42 ÷ 7 and 48 ÷ 8, saying the multiplication question first, then have her retake (she gets a brand-new set of questions). Monday's practice set and packet are on Tuesday's task list, not tonight's. Tuesday builds directly on today: fact triangles become full fact families.

tasks: Monday night: do the After-class lesson. It ends with Show What You Know. You need 90.
Monday night: read How to Train Your Dragon for 10 minutes. Find one new word to share on Tuesday.

slides.title: Division Undoes Multiplication
slides.text: You already know your 6, 7, 8 and 9 facts. Today you find out they work backward too. Division asks a multiplication question with a missing number, so the facts you know are the key.

notes.do: Share your screen. Before you start, check that Bailey has at her table: about 45 dried beans, 6 cups or paper plates, 6 index cards, a pencil and her book. Keep your whiteboard in view of your camera.
notes.say: "Last week you stopped adding and started multiplying. This week we run multiplication backward. By the end of today you will solve 56 ÷ 8 without adding a single 8."
notes.ask: "What is 8 × 7?" (56). "Hold on to that. You will use it in ten minutes."

slides.title: Back to Berk
slides.text: Think about How to Train Your Dragon.
prompts: Tell me what happened in the last chapter you read. Keep the events in order.
What problem is Hiccup facing right now? Is he up against another character, himself, or nature?
Find one word the author used that was new or interesting to you. What do you think it means, and what clue helped you?
starters: I think the word … means … because …

notes.do: Give her the whole 7 minutes. Let her hold the book and find pages.
notes.say: "Book first. Tell me the last chapter in order: first, next, then, last."
notes.ask: After the retell: "What kind of conflict is Hiccup in: against another character, himself, or nature? Prove it with one event." Then: "Show me one new word and the clue you used."
notes.listen: A strong answer names the conflict type AND gives an event as proof. If she only says "he has a problem", ask: "With whom or with what?"

slides.title: Facts you will need today
slides.text: Say each answer out loud as fast as you can. Jonathan types it in.

items.no: Use double, double, double: 7, 14, 28, 56.
Use the ×9 shortcut: 10 × 6, then take away one 6.
Use the ×6 shortcut: 5 × 7, then add one more 7.
Use the ×9 shortcut: 10 × 7, then take away one 7.

notes.do: Type her spoken answers into the boxes yourself (she is on Zoom, so she says them, you type). Time each one silently.
notes.say: "Four facts. Say the answer, then tell me which shortcut you used."
notes.listen: Under 3 seconds = automatic. If she starts counting up (8, 16, 24 …), stop her and ask for the shortcut from Lessons 1–4. These four facts are today's answers in disguise.

slides.title: Words for today
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read the word out loud, then make up your own sentence with it.

words.meaning: The number being divided: the total you start with.
The number you divide by: the number of groups, or how many go in each group.
The answer to a division problem.
Two operations that undo each other, like multiplication and division.
To give out something in small, set amounts so that it lasts longer.
words.example: When the winter was long, the Vikings had to ration their bread.

words.meaning: Supplies of food and other things people need, packed for later.
words.example: The ship carried provisions for a week at sea.

words.meaning: To give each person or group a certain share of something.
words.example: The chief will allot 6 arrows to each archer.

notes.do: Flip one card at a time. She reads the word and meaning aloud. On your whiteboard write dividend ÷ divisor = quotient above 56 ÷ 8 = 7 and draw an arrow from each word to its number. Leave it up for the whole lesson.
notes.say: "Four math words and three story words. The math words name the parts of a division and how × and ÷ undo each other. The story words are about sharing food and supplies, which is what division is."
notes.ask: For ration: "Why would Vikings ration food in winter?" For provisions: "What provisions would Hiccup pack to fly to another island?" For allot: "If Stoick allots 6 arrows to each archer, what operation tells how many arrows he needs?"
notes.listen: Her own sentence must show the meaning, not just use the word ("I rationed" is not enough; "We rationed the snacks so they lasted all trip" is). For inverse operations she should say they undo each other.

slides.title: Division question 1: How many in each?
slides.text: Stoick has 24 fish to share equally among 6 dragons. How many fish does each dragon get?

visual.sub: How many fish for each dragon?

steps.text: We know the number of groups: 6 dragons.
We want to find how many go in each group.
Think: 6 × ? = 24. 6 × 4 = 24, so 24 ÷ 6 = 4 fish for each dragon.

slides.tip: No counting one by one. A multiplication fact you know gives the answer.

notes.do: Hands-on at home: she counts out 24 beans and sets out 6 plates (the dragons). She deals one bean to each plate per round until the beans are gone. Hold the slide on the problem until she finishes, then reveal the steps.
notes.say: "Every plate is a dragon. Deal them like cards: one to each, then again."
notes.ask: "How many on each plate?" (4). "How many rounds did you deal?" (4). "So which fact did you just act out?" (6 × 4 = 24).
notes.listen: She should notice the number of rounds IS the answer. That is why the multiplication fact works.

slides.title: Division question 2: How many groups?
slides.text: Fishlegs has 24 fish. He puts 6 fish in each basket. How many baskets does he fill?

steps.text: We know how many go in each group: 6 fish.
We want to find how many groups.

slides.tip: Same numbers, two different questions. Read carefully to see which one the story asks.

notes.do: She gathers the 24 beans again and this time makes piles of exactly 6, one plate per pile, until the beans run out. Then reveal the steps.
notes.ask: "Same 24 beans, same 6, same answer 4. So what changed?" Wait for it. Then: "What does the 4 count this time?"
notes.listen: The answer is the label: last time 4 fish in each, this time 4 baskets. If she says "nothing changed", click Back to show the last picture (6 groups of 4), then Next to this one (4 groups of 6).

slides.title: What is missing from the story?

items.q: Hiccup has 30 fish. He gives 6 fish to each dragon. What does the story not tell you yet?
choices: How many fish does each dragon get?
items.why: You know the size of each group (6 fish). You find how many groups: how many dragons. 30 ÷ 6 = 5 dragons.
no: The story tells you that already: 30 fish.
The story tells you that already: 6 fish each.

items.q: Stoick splits 36 shields equally among 9 ships. What does the story not tell you yet?
choices: How many shields on each ship?
items.why: You know the number of groups (9 ships). You find how many in each: 36 ÷ 9 = 4 shields.
no: The story tells you: 9 ships.
The story tells you: 36 shields.

notes.say: Detective question: which numbers does the story give me, and which one is missing?
notes.ask: After each one: "Say the multiplication question for it." (6 × ? = 30; 9 × ? = 36.)
notes.listen: She should name the known number's job: "6 is how many in each" or "9 is the number of groups".

slides.title: 56 ÷ 8 means 8 × ? = 56
slides.text: Division and multiplication are inverse operations. Every division fact is a multiplication fact with a missing number.

steps.text: Step 1. Turn it into a multiplication question: 8 × ? = 56.
Step 2. Try a fact you know. 8 × 6 = 48. Too small. 8 × 7 = 56. Yes!

slides.tip: Do not add 8 + 8 + 8 … until you reach 56. Ask yourself: 8 times what is 56?

notes.say: "This is the big idea of the whole week. Read it with me: fifty-six divided by eight means eight times WHAT is fifty-six."
notes.ask: Before Step 2: "Which 8s fact do you know that lands near 56?" Before Step 3: "Look back at the warm-up. Did you already say this fact today?"
notes.listen: "8 × 7 = 56, so it's 7." If she starts counting by 8s, say: "Counting works, but it is the slow road. Which fact jumps straight there?"

slides.title: Your turn to lead: 72 ÷ 9
slides.text: Solve 72 ÷ 9 the new way. Say each step out loud before you show it.

steps.text: So 72 ÷ 9 = 8. Adding nines would have taken 8 steps. The fact took one.

notes.say: "Now you are the teacher. Tell me the first step before I show it."
notes.ask: "What is the multiplication question?" "Which shortcut helps test 9 × 8?" "How many nines would you have added the slow way?" (8).
notes.listen: She says the question first, without prompting. That habit is what we are building today.

slides.title: Reading a fact triangle
slides.text: A fact triangle holds three numbers that work together. The top number is the biggest: it is the product of the two bottom numbers. Cover one corner and say the fact that finds it.
slides.tip: In a division fact from a triangle, the top number always comes first.

notes.do: Hands-on: she makes three index-card fact triangles while you watch: 8, 7, 56 · 7, 9, 63 · 6, 9, 54, biggest number at the top. Then you cover a corner on your screen and she says the fact; then she covers a corner on her card and quizzes you.
notes.ask: "Cover the top. Which operation finds it?" (multiply). "Cover a bottom corner. Which operation finds it?" (divide).
notes.listen: Division facts that start with the top number: "63 ÷ 7", never "7 ÷ 63". Tell Tia she keeps these three cards for Tuesday.

slides.title: Ask the multiplication question
slides.text: Say the multiplication question out loud. Then say the answer.

items.no: Use the ×6 shortcut: 5 × 8 = 40, plus one more 8.
Which 7s fact is near 63? 7 × 8 = 56 is close.

items.q: What number is hiding in this fact triangle?
items.no: Ask: 9 × what = 54?

items.q: Toothless has 63 shiny pebbles. He makes piles with 7 in each pile. Which fact tells how many piles?
no: Check that fact: 7 × 8 = 56, not 63.
Subtracting one 7 only makes one pile. How many sevens fit in 63?
Adding makes more pebbles. Piles split the 63 up.

notes.do: She answers out loud; you type. Do not move on from an item until she has said the full multiplication question, not just the number.
notes.listen: "Six times eight is forty-eight, so it's eight." On the pebbles item, ask her to explain why 8 piles is wrong (7 × 8 = 56).

slides.title: Feeding time on Berk
slides.text: Stoick shares 42 fish equally among 6 dragons. Make the groups: how many dragons, and how many fish for each one?
slides.why: 6 groups of 7 make 42. So 42 ÷ 6 = 7 fish for each dragon.
slides.hint: There are 6 dragons, so make 6 groups. Then ask: 6 × what = 42?

notes.do: Before anyone touches a bean, she predicts the answer with a fact. Then she proves it: 42 beans onto 6 plates. Then you set the counters on screen to her answer.
notes.ask: "Prediction first: 6 times what is 42?" After the beans: "Did your fact match your plates?"
notes.listen: "6 × 7 = 42, so 7 each." If she predicts wrong, the beans will show it. Let them.

slides.title: Name the parts, spot the mistake

items.q: In 72 ÷ 8 = 9, which number is the quotient?
no: 72 is the dividend, the number being divided.
8 is the divisor, the number you divide by.

items.q: In 42 ÷ 7 = 6, the number 42 is called the ____.
items.why: The dividend is the number being divided: 42.
items.no: Look at the whiteboard: dividend ÷ divisor = quotient. Which spot is 42 in?

items.q: Snotlout says 63 ÷ 7 = 8 because 7 × 8 = 63. What is wrong?
choices: You can't use multiplication to solve division.
items.why: 7 × 9 = 63, so 63 ÷ 7 = 9. Snotlout used a wrong fact.
no: You can! They are inverse operations. His fact was just wrong.
Adding does not undo multiplication. Division does.

notes.say: "Point to the whiteboard while you answer."
notes.ask: On the Snotlout item: "How could he have caught his own mistake?" (Check 7 × 8 with the ×7 shortcut: 40 + 16 = 56, not 63.)
notes.listen: Divisor and quotient are the pair she mixes up. Make her say the sentence: "The divisor is what I divide BY."

slides.title: Say the fact, then the quotient
slides.text: For each card: say the multiplication fact out loud, then the quotient.

items.no: 7 × what = 42?
Double, double, double 8.
6 × what = 36?
7 × what = 49?

notes.do: She says the fact and the quotient; you type the quotient. Keep the pace quick, like flash cards.
notes.say: "Fact first, then the answer. Ready? Go."
notes.listen: Fast, confident facts on 42 ÷ 7, 54 ÷ 9 and 56 ÷ 8. A pause on 64 ÷ 8 is fine: prompt "double, double, double 8". If she counts up by the divisor, stop and ask for the fact.

items.q: Before the voyage, Stoick packed provisions into the longship. What did he pack?
items.why: Provisions are supplies of food and needed things, packed for later.
no: Provisions are mostly food and needed supplies, not just one thing.
That would be a hoard, not provisions.
Provisions are what people need to live: food, water, supplies.

items.q: The chief had to allot the shields fairly. What does allot mean here?
items.why: To allot is to give each person a certain share.
no: Counting is not the same as handing out shares.
That is the opposite: allot means to give out.

items.q: When food is low, you give it out in small, set amounts so it lasts. You ____ it. (Use a word from your word cards.)
items.why: To ration is to give out small, set amounts so supplies last.
items.no: It starts with r. The Vikings did it to their bread in winter.

notes.ask: "Which word in the sentence was your clue?" (packed into the longship; fairly; lasts). Then: "Which of today's story words is most like division?" (allot or ration: both split a total into shares.)
notes.listen: She connects allot to "how many in each". That link is the reason these words were chosen.
